analysis.one_liner: Creates a mandatory federal inspection program for seafood to keep adulterated or mislabeled fish off the market.
analysis.headline: Backed by 29 bipartisan cosponsors and approved by the House Agriculture Committee in July 1990, the bill died without ever receiving a House floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put all seafood processing under a federal inspection program run by the Secretary of Agriculture, similar to the mandatory inspection meat and poultry already had. Processing plants and vessels would have to register and pass inspection, labels would need government approval, imports would have to meet the same U.S. standards, and violators would face civil and criminal penalties. Despite bipartisan sponsorship and approval by the House Agriculture Committee, the bill never got a vote on the House floor before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would get the same federal protection from contaminated or deceptively labeled seafood that meat and poultry already had under laws the bill itself cites. Honest seafood processors and the nation's fish farmers would also benefit, because the bill's findings say adulterated and mislabeled seafood sells more cheaply and competes unfairly against wholesome product. States would receive federal grants covering half the cost of monitoring fishing areas and running their own inspection programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seafood consumers and honest seafood producers

how_it_helps.text: No plant or vessel could process seafood without registering with the Secretary of Agriculture, and inspectors could enter facilities at any time, sample product, and detain or condemn seafood found to be adulterated or misbranded.

Imported seafood would have to meet the same U.S. standards as domestic product, and no seafood could enter from a country whose inspection program was not certified as at least equal to the U.S. program.

Selling or transporting adulterated or misbranded seafood would carry civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and criminal penalties including up to three years in prison for knowing distribution of adulterated product.

States would get federal grants covering 50 percent of the cost of monitoring fishing production areas and of running their own certified inspection programs, plus a national seafood safety education program.

The bill's findings state that unwholesome and deceptively packaged seafood sells at lower prices and competes unfairly with wholesome product, to the detriment of the public and of producers, including fish farmers; the inspection program was designed to end that unfair competition.

analysis.who_pays: Seafood processing plants and vessels would pay registration, inspection, recordkeeping, and label-preapproval costs, and would destroy product found adulterated. Importers and foreign suppliers would bear the cost of meeting U.S. standards and of storage and destruction costs for refused shipments. Taxpayers would fund the federal inspection system, which the bill authorizes at 'such sums as are necessary' with no fiscal-year limit. Some costs would likely reach consumers through higher seafood prices.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy: every establishment and vessel must register, keep detailed records open to government inspection, and submit every label and package design to the Secretary for approval before use, costs that fall hardest on small processors and would be partly passed to consumers.

The bill leaves real gaps: vessels that only head, gut, skin, shuck, ice, freeze, or brine-chill fish are exempt pending a future study, and traditional retail and restaurant processing is exempt, so some parts of the supply chain stay uninspected.

It preempts state rules: states could not impose any marking, labeling, package, or ingredient requirements on registered establishments different from the federal ones, taking away stricter state food-safety rules.

The program would sit under the Secretary of Agriculture through the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, a marketing statute, rather than the existing federal food-safety framework under the Food and Drug Administration that already had jurisdiction over seafood.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit was real: at the time, meat and poultry had mandatory federal inspection but seafood did not, and the bill would have closed that gap with detention and condemnation powers, import controls, and penalties. The cost was a new compliance system whose expense fell on processors, vessels, and importers, with the design questions an honest supporter would have to concede: every label needed pre-approval, the preemption clause wiped out stricter state rules, and large parts of the harvesting and retail chain were exempted pending study. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the costs, but the bill as written was a blunt and paperwork-heavy instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The House Agriculture Committee approved the bill in July 1990, but House leadership never scheduled it for a floor vote, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 23, 1989 by Rep. E. de la Garza with 22 bipartisan original cosponsors and was referred jointly to the Agriculture and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees.
The committees requested comments from the USDA, Commerce, and HHS agencies, and a subcommittee held hearings on November 9, 1989.
On July 18, 1990 the House Agriculture Committee met, marked the bill up, and ordered it reported as amended, meaning a majority of the committee approved sending it to the floor.
No floor action followed; the bill never received a House vote, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seafood processors, fishing vessels, and importers came out ahead, avoiding new registration, inspection, and label-approval costs. Consumers came out without the mandatory seafood inspection program the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 29 cosponsors split 20 Democrats and 9 Republicans, the original introduction included members of both parties, and the bill cleared committee with no recorded opposition; it failed for lack of floor time, not a recorded vote.

industries.note: They would bear registration, inspection, recordkeeping, and label-preapproval costs, but the bill's own findings say adulterated and mislabeled seafood undercuts honest processors, so mandatory inspection also protected their markets and consumer confidence.

Imports would have to meet U.S. standards, and no seafood could enter from a country without a certified equivalent inspection program, with refused shipments destroyed at the owner's expense; their interest in keeping low-cost, lightly inspected product flowing ran against the consumer protections.

Vessels doing only basic handling such as heading, gutting, icing, or freezing were exempt pending a study of whether they should be included, while vessels doing more extensive processing would have registered and faced inspection.
The bill's findings say farmers engaged in aquaculture were hurt when adulterated seafood competed unfairly, so the inspection program protected their market alongside consumers.
The bill gave the Secretary of Agriculture a new permanent seafood program with open-ended funding and rulemaking, subpoena, and penalty powers, expanding the department's jurisdiction over food.
Operations traditionally conducted at retail stores and restaurants were exempt from the program, sparing them compliance costs, though that exemption left part of the chain uninspected.
